title: The clever sage
hook: Mahosadha solves the court's riddles and saves the kingdom by wit (Jataka 546)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vidhura, the pandita, was won at dice and taught the spirit who carried him off. Your line was he taught his captor. Did you offer something useful where you didn't choose to be? Today, a boy who solves things. Day eight hundred forty-six.

Two women, one baby, and a judge who is still a child. Each woman swears the baby is hers. Nobody saw what happened. In the Jataka the judge is a village boy named Mahosadha, who has built a hall where people bring their quarrels, and this is one of them. He doesn't ask for witnesses. He draws a line on the ground. Today, what the line is for, and how a boy's wit ends up saving a kingdom.
screen: `TWO WOMEN, ONE BABY.` → `A BOY JUDGE.` → `A LINE ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the name. The story says he was born holding a healing herb, and so he was called Mahosadha, great medicine. It's a fitting name for someone whose gift is fixing things. Second, the cases. Back to the line. He places the baby on it and tells the women to pull, one by the arms, one by the legs; whoever pulls the child across keeps him. They pull. The baby cries out. And one woman lets go, rather than hurt him. That, the boy says, is the mother. The other, the story reveals, wasn't human at all. Case after case goes like that: he finds the answer by watching how people act, not by guessing. Third, the court. Word reaches King Vedeha of Mithila, who brings the boy to court. There, jealous advisers test him, scheme against him, try to get him thrown out. He keeps answering riddles, keeps seeing through traps. Fourth, the kingdom. When a rival king threatens Mithila, Mahosadha's plan, a great tunnel, the ummagga the tale is named for, turns a trap into a peace and saves his king. Tradition pairs this tale with wisdom, panna. What's notable is the kind of wisdom. It's practical. It reads people. And it's always used to protect someone: the baby, the cheated, the king. The baby goes home with the woman who let go.
screen: `BORN HOLDING A HEALING HERB.` · `THE MOTHER LETS GO.` · `RIDDLES AND TRAPS AT COURT.` · `A GREAT TUNNEL SAVES THE KING.` · then, large: `WIT THAT SAVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch, don't guess. Rest your hands and let the room go quiet. Bring to mind one person whose mood or need you've been guessing at lately. A child, a coworker, a friend who's gone quiet. Set the guesses aside. Recall only what they actually did this week: what they reached for, what they avoided, when they lit up. Let their actions tell you something, the way the mother's letting go told Mahosadha. Find one small, practical way to help that fits what you saw. The bell holds the time.
Panna. Wisdom: what Mahosadha the boy judge showed, reading people well and using his wit to protect them, all the way to saving his king. Today's word.
Your line: wit that saves. Try the one small help you found, and watch what the person does, not just what they say. Day eight hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: The Mahosadha story is told as a tale of practical wisdom; in Buddhist teaching, wisdom (panna) is one of the ten perfections.

fork.setup: you're the boy judge. two women each claim the baby, and no one saw what happened. what do you do?

set a test that shows who loves the child.
send them away to the king.

original.note: Pali panna, wisdom: the perfection tradition pairs with Mahosadha's tale.

trapdoor: what you thought: a book of riddles with a clever boy.
what it means: practical wisdom that reads people and is always used to protect someone, from a baby to a king.
what a scholar hears: Jataka 546, also called the Maha-ummagga, the great tunnel, takes its name from the tunnel that ends it, and tradition pairs it with panna.

sources.ref: Jataka 546 (Mahaummagga Jataka, the tale of Mahosadha)

notes: Confirm: born holding a medicinal herb and named for it (the text gives this reason); the hall he built; the child case (the false claimant a yakkhini); King Vedeha; jealous court sages (the text names four; number omitted); the tunnel against King Culani Brahmadatta.
Confirm the traditional pairing Mahosadha = panna (wisdom).
The child case resembles stories in other traditions; deliberately not compared.
Editor: replaced the closing aphorism with a concrete detail from the tale; fixed a double comma in the trapdoor.
Audit: practice and carry rewritten; the old 'two people pulling, sit with both sides' practice repeated day 835's quarrel practice. New angle: read people by their actions, as Mahosadha does.
